R package · companion to gstat

fastkcv

Fast, exact cross-validation for global kriging

kcv() takes the same inputs as gstat::krige.cv() and returns the same output. It factorizes the covariance matrix of the observations once, instead of refitting the kriging system for every fold, and the results agree with krige.cv() to numerical precision.

Installation

Using pak:

pak::pkg_install("n-c-taylor/fastkcv")

Using remotes:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("n-c-taylor/fastkcv", build_vignettes = TRUE)

The package contains C++ code, so installing from GitHub needs a compiler toolchain: Rtools on Windows, the Xcode command line tools on macOS.

Example 

library(fastkcv)
library(gstat)
data(meuse, package = "sp")
v <- vgm(0.59, "Sph", 897, 0.05)

# Leave-one-out, as krige.cv(log(zinc) ~ 1, ~ x + y, meuse, model = v)
cv <- kcv(log(zinc) ~ 1, ~ x + y, meuse, model = v)
kcv_metrics(cv)

# One factorization, several fold designs
p <- kcv_prepare(log(zinc) ~ sqrt(dist), ~ x + y, meuse, model = v)
set.seed(1)
kcv_metrics(kcv_run(p, folds = fold_random(~ x + y, meuse, k = 10)))
kcv_metrics(kcv_run(p, folds = fold_blocks(~ x + y, meuse, blocks = 3)))
kcv_metrics(kcv_run(p, buffer = 300))

Performance

Ordinary kriging on simulated data, 4-core laptop with OpenBLAS (median seconds; from the scripts in inst/bench/):

n LOO: fastkcv / krige.cv() 5-fold: fastkcv / krige.cv()
1,000 0.06 / 67 (1,100x) 0.07 / 0.8 (12x)
2,000 0.25 / 368 (1,500x) 0.29 / 5.7 (19x)
5,000 2.1 / not run 2.6 / 85 (32x)

The gain is largest for leave-one-out and smallest for a few large folds. kcv() handles n = 20,000 in about two minutes.

The vignette (Get started) covers the fold designs, buffered leave-one-out, precomputed covariance matrices, and the performance and memory notes.

Scope

Global kriging only: every observation is in the kriging neighborhood. Local neighborhoods (nmax, nmin, maxdist), block kriging, unbounded variograms, geographic coordinates and re-fitting the variogram in each fold are not supported, and give an error. Memory is one n x n matrix (8 n^2 bytes, 3.2 GB at n = 20,000), checked before anything is allocated.

Related packages

fastkcv is a companion to gstat, not a fork or a replacement: kcv() takes the inputs of krige.cv() and returns its output, and fitting variograms and kriging new locations stay with gstat. It is a separate package for three reasons. The single factorization works only for global kriging, while gstat’s engine sets up a kriging system for each prediction location, which is what makes local neighborhoods (nmax, maxdist) possible. It needs compiled C++ code (Rcpp, RcppArmadillo) and a dense n x n matrix (8 n^2 bytes, checked up front). And most of the package is a cross-validation toolkit rather than a faster krige.cv(): buffered leave-one-out, spatial fold builders, kcv_metrics(), kcv_prepare() / kcv_run() to reuse one factorization, and kcv_engine() for any covariance matrix.

leaveOneOut.km() in DiceKriging uses the same closed-form leave-one-out algebra, without a nugget term, with tensor-product kernels on a design matrix rather than gstat variogram models on spatial data, and without k-fold or buffered designs. From the same covariance matrix, fastkcv is 1.6 to 4.1 times faster end to end (OpenBLAS) and about level on the leave-one-out step alone. blockCV and spatialsample build spatial folds for any model but do not fit one; a partition from them, such as folds_ids from blockCV’s cv_spatial(), can be passed to kcv_run(folds = ).

Use of AI tools

This package was developed with the help of an AI coding assistant (Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5), used for writing and reviewing code, tests and documentation. The author directed the work and is responsible for the package; its results are checked against gstat::krige.cv() and independent R implementations by the test suite.
